summary: Second round on the invoice CSV export: who, which invoices, columns, number format.

questions.title: Who exports
questions.ask: Who gets the export button: everyone who can see invoices, or only admins?
questions.context: Settles who the feature is for, which decides whether it needs a new permission or rides on the existing invoice access.
questions.recommendation: Everyone who can see the invoice list; the export holds exactly what they can already see.
questions.why: The invoice list already filters by permission (InvoiceQuery.visible_to), so the export inherits it and needs no new rule.

questions.title: Which invoices
questions.ask: Does the export take the invoices currently filtered on screen, or all of them?
questions.context: Settles how big an export can get, which decides whether it streams from the request or needs a background job.
questions.recommendation: The current filter, so what you see is what you get.
questions.why: A full export of 40k invoices would need a background job; the filtered list is capped at 5,000 rows and can stream straight from the request.

questions.title: Columns
questions.ask: Which columns go in the file?
questions.context: Settles what the file promises to hold, so accounting can rely on it when reconciling.
questions.recommendation: The columns visible in the table, in the same order, plus the invoice id and the customer's org number.
questions.why: Accounting asked for the org number (Vault: 'Invoice reconciliation'). Matching the table keeps the file predictable; the id makes every row traceable back to its invoice.

questions.title: Number format
questions.ask: Should amounts use Norwegian formatting (1 234,50) or plain (1234.50)?
questions.context: Settles whether the file opens cleanly in Excel and imports cleanly elsewhere.
questions.recommendation: Plain 1234.50 with a period, and UTF-8 with a BOM so Excel opens æøå correctly.
questions.why: Plain numbers survive every importer; the BOM is the one Excel quirk that matters for Norwegian names.
